title: Certified Kubernetes Administrator (CKA) Cluster Operations & Maintenance
summary: Master CKA cluster operations: safe node maintenance (cordon, drain, uncordon, taints), control-plane lifecycle upgrades via kubeadm, and etcd disaster recovery snapshot management.
learningObjectives: Execute safe worker node maintenance procedures using kubectl cordon, drain with daemonset tolerations, taints, and uncordon.
Perform end-to-end Kubernetes control plane version upgrades using kubeadm upgrade plan and apply workflows.
Execute disaster recovery snapshots and integrity audits of the distributed etcd datastore using etcdctl snapshot tools.

curriculumModules.title: Node Maintenance: Cordon, Drain, Uncordon, Taints & Tolerations
curriculumModules.conceptSummary: Node lifecycle management allows administrators to isolate worker nodes for OS patching, kernel upgrades, or hardware maintenance. Cordoning marks a node unschedulable. Draining evicts existing workloads respecting PodDisruptionBudgets. Taints repel pods lacking matching tolerations.
curriculumModules.productionArchitecturePattern: Always specify --ignore-daemonsets during drains because DaemonSets are managed per-node and will block drain indefinitely. Configure PodDisruptionBudgets (PDBs) to ensure high-availability quorum is maintained during maintenance windows.

curriculumModules.title: Control Plane Lifecycle: Kubeadm Upgrades & Static Pod Management
curriculumModules.conceptSummary: Kubernetes control plane components run as static pods supervised directly by kubelet in /etc/kubernetes/manifests. kubeadm streamlines zero-downtime upgrades across control plane nodes, validating component versions, certificates, and API deprecations.
curriculumModules.productionArchitecturePattern: Never upgrade worker nodes before control-plane nodes. Always upgrade sequentially one minor version at a time (e.g., v1.31 -> v1.32), and take an etcd snapshot immediately prior to running kubeadm upgrade apply.

curriculumModules.title: Disaster Recovery: Etcdctl Snapshot Backup & Quorum Restoration
curriculumModules.conceptSummary: etcd is the single source of truth for all Kubernetes cluster state. etcdctl provides atomic point-in-time snapshot creation and verification. In disaster scenarios, restoring an etcd snapshot reconstructs all API resources and namespaces across the cluster.
curriculumModules.productionArchitecturePattern: Automate hourly etcdctl snapshot saves to encrypted object storage, monitor etcd disk fsync latency (< 10ms threshold), and test bare-metal restoration drills in staging clusters periodically.

labs.title: Zero-Downtime Worker Node Maintenance: Cordon, Drain & Taints
labs.scenario: Perform an operational maintenance drill on worker node kubelabs-worker-01: cordon the node to stop new pod scheduling, safely drain existing workloads while ignoring DaemonSets, apply a maintenance taint dedicated=special:NoSchedule, and uncordon the node after maintenance completes.
labs.productionContext: Operating Kubernetes in production requires executing kernel patches and hardware upgrades without interrupting customer traffic, requiring safe eviction and node cordoning workflows.
objectives: Cordon worker node kubelabs-worker-01 to mark it unschedulable
Uncordon worker node to resume normal scheduling

labs.title: Cluster Disaster Recovery & Kubeadm Control-Plane Lifecycle
labs.scenario: Execute a critical disaster recovery snapshot of the etcd datastore before planning and applying a control-plane upgrade to v1.32.0 using kubeadm.
labs.productionContext: Taking a verified etcd snapshot before executing kubeadm control-plane upgrades is a non-negotiable CKA operational best practice that guarantees cluster rollback capability.

assessmentQuestions.question: Why is the --ignore-daemonsets flag typically required when executing kubectl drain on a worker node?
options: (Recommended) DaemonSets manage pods on every node automatically, so evicting a DaemonSet pod causes its controller to immediately recreate it, preventing the drain command from ever completing.
DaemonSets run directly in the Linux kernel and cannot be stopped by the kubelet.
DaemonSets do not use network namespaces and cannot be evicted.
The --ignore-daemonsets flag bypasses RBAC permission checks on the cluster.
assessmentQuestions.explanation: DaemonSets run an instance of a Pod on all matching nodes. If kubectl drain attempts to evict a DaemonSet-managed Pod, the DaemonSet controller immediately creates a replacement Pod on that same node. Therefore, kubectl drain requires --ignore-daemonsets to explicitly bypass DaemonSet pods.

assessmentQuestions.question: When performing an etcd snapshot restore using 'etcdctl snapshot restore', what is the recommended procedure regarding the kube-apiserver?
options: (Recommended) Stop all kube-apiserver instances before restoring the snapshot to prevent write skew and conflicting mutations, then restart kube-apiserver pointing to the restored data directory.
Leave kube-apiserver running so it can coordinate the restore across all worker nodes.
Delete all Namespaces using kubectl delete ns --all before running the restore.
Scale the etcd cluster to zero replicas using kubectl scale.
assessmentQuestions.explanation: To prevent split-brain conditions or writes occurring during snapshot restoration, all kube-apiserver instances must be temporarily stopped (e.g., moving static pod manifests out of /etc/kubernetes/manifests). After etcdctl snapshot restore initializes the new data directory, kube-apiserver is restarted.
